strengths: The paper proposes a simple, parameter-free architectural change: during SFT, modify the attention mask so earlier image tokens can attend to later question tokens while response generation remains causal. This is easy to integrate into existing decoder-only MLLM pipelines and is a useful design point for the community.

The main apples-to-apples experiment is reasonably convincing: under matched backbone, connector, data, and training schedule, MMA improves over the conventional image-then-text pipeline, dual-order training variants, and the closely related CCA baseline on 11/12 benchmarks, with especially large gains on MME cognition, MMB, LLaVA-Bench, MMMU, and CV-Bench.

The paper includes broad evaluation across general, knowledge, and vision-centric benchmarks, plus detailed appendix breakdowns, prompt templates, dataset statistics, and training hyperparameters. This makes the empirical story easier to audit than many MLLM papers.

The limitations section identifies a real technical constraint: applying MMA during pretraining can leak future text through image tokens, so the method is currently restricted to SFT-style inputs with a clear question prefix.
weaknesses: The central causal explanation is only partially established. The experiments show that the mask change improves downstream scores, but there is little mechanistic evidence that the gains specifically come from image tokens using question information, rather than distributional effects, optimization changes, or interactions with the SFT templates.

Novelty is moderate. The method resembles prefix-LM / bidirectional-context attention masks and general non-causal attention over conditioning inputs, adapted to MLLMs. The paper should position the contribution more carefully relative to existing mask designs and multimodal prefix conditioning.

Some claims are overstated. Table 2 does not show AKI-4B being broadly superior to similar-size open-source/proprietary models across most benchmarks; it is best on only a subset and is clearly behind BLIP-3, Qwen2-VL, Phi-3-Vision, or MiniCPM on several metrics.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful details. The abstract has a blank code URL, the model is only promised for future release, no seeds or variance estimates are reported, and the large-scale AKI-4B comparison relies on heterogeneous external leaderboard/paper numbers rather than fully controlled reruns.

The masking implementation details for teacher-forced SFT need sharper specification. Since answer tokens are present during training, the paper should explicitly prove or document that image/question tokens cannot attend to target response tokens and that no label leakage occurs in practical batching/KV-cache handling.

The broader-impact and ethics discussion is quite generic for an MLLM that may reduce hallucination but can still produce misleading visual answers. The paper does not discuss failure modes, deployment risks, benchmark contamination, or data provenance concerns in much depth.

strengths: The paper identifies a real architectural issue in decoder-only MLLMs: image tokens placed before text cannot directly condition on the user query under a standard causal mask. The proposed mask modification is simple, parameter-free, and easy to integrate in principle.

The authors attempt an apples-to-apples comparison in Section 4.2 against a causal baseline, CCA, and dual-order variants using the same backbone, datasets, and training schedules. This is the most useful part of the paper.
The appendix includes useful implementation details such as backbone choices, training hyperparameters, dataset sampling ratios, prompt templates, and benchmark prompt formats.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not sufficiently reliable. Several reported numbers are internally inconsistent: Table 1 reports MMA MMEP as 1363.7, while Appendix Table 7 sums to 1344.9; Table 1 reports MMA MMB as 71.8, while Appendix Table 8 reports 70.3; Appendix Table 8 also reports AKI-4B relation reasoning as 0.65, which appears inconsistent with the surrounding percentage scale. These inconsistencies undermine confidence in the evaluation.

The scaled AKI-4B comparison does not isolate the proposed contribution. AKI-4B uses a longer schedule and additional OCR pretraining data, but there is no matched full-schedule causal-attention baseline with the same data. Therefore the paper cannot attribute the final model’s performance to MMA rather than data, OCR training, or longer optimization.

The state-of-the-art comparison is overstated. AKI-4B is worse than several 3B/4B models on many metrics, including MMB, SEED, MMMU, MathVista, POPE, MM-Vet, RealWorldQA, and CV-Bench, yet the text claims broadly superior or highly remarkable performance. The comparison mixes leaderboard, paper-reported, and self-evaluated numbers under different resolutions, datasets, and training budgets, so it is not a convincing SOTA result.

The method is evaluated on only one architecture family/backbone in the controlled setting, despite claims of generic applicability to MLLMs, other modalities, interleaved data, and hierarchical inputs. These broader claims are speculative and not experimentally supported.

The paper lacks important ablations: MMA during training only vs inference only, which layers receive the modified mask, whether image tokens may attend to system/question/answer tokens, sensitivity to image-token count, prompt format, sequence order, and whether the improvement comes from query-conditioned visual representations rather than the proposed causal-attention framing.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract contains a blank code URL, the model is promised for future release, random seeds/variance are not reported, and the large-scale training recipe depends on substantial compute. The appendix helps, but not enough to reproduce the claimed results reliably.

The limitations and ethics discussion is thin. It acknowledges PT-stage leakage but does not analyze possible leakage paths during SFT teacher forcing, does not discuss benchmark/data contamination despite no deduplication, and does not address safety risks from more confident multimodal hallucinations.

Presentation is often imprecise or overclaimed. The paper repeatedly describes the contribution as fundamental and unexplored, but related designs such as non-causal/prefix/bidirectional attention in multimodal encoders and query-conditioned visual processing are not sufficiently discussed. Some qualitative examples are anecdotal and do not compensate for the quantitative issues.

strengths: The paper identifies a simple and plausible architectural bottleneck in decoder-only MLLMs: with image-before-text prompting, causal attention prevents visual tokens from conditioning on the user query. The proposed modality-mutual attention is technically clean, parameter-free, and easy to integrate into existing MLLM training pipelines.

The empirical section is strong. The authors provide controlled apples-to-apples comparisons against the conventional image-text pipeline, CCA, and multiple dual-order training variants using the same backbone, datasets, and schedules. MMA improves over CCA on 11 of 12 reported benchmarks, with especially large gains on MME cognition, LLaVA-Bench, MMMU, and MM-Vet.

The evaluation spans a broad set of general, knowledge, and vision-centric benchmarks, and the appendix includes useful per-category breakdowns, prompt templates, dataset mixtures, hyperparameters, training duration, and decoding settings. This makes the empirical claims more interpretable and reasonably reproducible.

The work is significant because the method is inexpensive and addresses a real practical issue in multimodal LLMs. Even if the idea is conceptually simple, the consistent benchmark improvements suggest it could be a useful default design choice for future MLLMs.

The limitations section honestly discusses an important failure mode: applying MMA during pretraining can create information leakage through image tokens. This is a meaningful caveat rather than a superficial limitation.
weaknesses: The exact SFT attention masking protocol is under-specified. The paper says image tokens attend to question text tokens and generated response tokens use standard causal attention, but in teacher-forced SFT the full prompt-answer sequence is available unless carefully masked. A clearer implementation-level description is needed to rule out answer-token leakage during training.

The broader generality claims are stronger than the evidence. The method is evaluated only for image-text single-image settings, while claims about audio, interleaved multimodal data, hierarchical inputs, and arbitrary modality combinations remain speculative.

The comparison to state-of-the-art models in Table 2 is less conclusive than the controlled study. AKI-4B is competitive but not uniformly superior among 3B-4B models, and differences in pretraining data, image resolution, token counts, and evaluation sources make these comparisons hard to interpret causally.

No variance estimates, multiple seeds, or significance testing are reported. Given the cost of training this is understandable, but it leaves some uncertainty about the reliability of smaller gains, such as the 1-4% improvements on several benchmarks.

Reproducibility is mostly good in the appendix, but the abstract appears to have a missing code URL and the model is promised for future release rather than available at submission time. Exact implementation details for MMA in the KV cache and SFT loss/mask construction should be included.

The research ethics discussion is fairly thin. Since the work improves MLLM reliability and uses large web-derived datasets, it would benefit from more discussion of dataset provenance, biases, hallucination risks, and possible misuse of more capable multimodal systems.
